meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering D1.1 DNA replication, guide topic D1.1.
final_note: You worked through D1.1 DNA replication — 9 guide statements.

concepts.def: The production of exact copies of a DNA molecule, each with a base sequence identical to the original, before a cell divides. It is required for reproduction, so that offspring receive the genetic material, and in multicellular organisms for growth and for the replacement of tissues, because every new cell produced by cell division must receive a complete copy of the DNA.

The order of the bases (A, T, C and G) along a strand of DNA, which carries the genetic information. Two DNA molecules with identical base sequences carry identical information, so an exact copy of DNA means a copy with an identical base sequence, not merely one of the same length or base composition.

The mode of DNA replication in which the two strands of the parent molecule separate and each acts as a template for a new strand, so that each of the two daughter molecules consists of one original (conserved) strand and one newly synthesized strand. Because every new strand is built directly against an original strand, the original base sequence is retained in each copy.

The rule that adenine pairs only with thymine and guanine only with cytosine, through hydrogen bonds between the bases. During replication a free nucleotide is held in position on the template only if its base is complementary to the template base, so the base sequence of each new strand is dictated by the template and copying is highly accurate.

An original strand of DNA against which a new strand is assembled. The new strand is complementary to the template, not identical to it; it is therefore identical in sequence to the strand that was originally paired with the template. Both strands of a DNA molecule act as templates during replication.

The enzyme that unwinds the DNA double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the two strands so that each can act as a template. Helicase does not break the covalent bonds of the sugar–phosphate backbone, so each strand remains intact.

The enzyme that assembles a new strand of DNA on a template strand. It links free DNA nucleotides, whose bases have paired with complementary bases on the template, into a growing strand by forming covalent bonds between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next. The hydrogen bonds between complementary bases are not made by the enzyme.

A laboratory technique for amplifying (making very many copies of) a chosen section of DNA. Each cycle uses temperature changes: heating to about 95°C separates the strands by breaking hydrogen bonds, cooling to about 50–65°C lets primers anneal to the template, and warming to about 72°C lets Taq polymerase extend each primer. The number of copies doubles every cycle, so about thirty cycles give more than a billion copies from a single molecule.

A short single-stranded piece of DNA, added to the reaction, whose sequence is complementary to one end of the target section. Two primers are used, one for each strand, binding either side of the target. They give DNA polymerase a starting point, because the enzyme can only extend an existing strand, and their positions define which section of the DNA is amplified.

A DNA polymerase from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, which lives in hot springs. It is heat-stable, so it is not denatured by the high temperature used to separate the DNA strands in each PCR cycle and does not have to be replaced. Its optimum temperature is about 72°C, which is the temperature used for the extension step.

A technique for separating DNA fragments by length. Samples are placed in wells in a gel and a voltage is applied. DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so all fragments move towards the positive electrode; smaller fragments pass through the pores of the gel more easily and travel further in a given time, so the fragments separate into bands in order of size.

The comparison of the patterns of DNA fragments produced from different individuals at a set of variable regions (markers). Sections are amplified by PCR and separated by gel electrophoresis, giving a pattern of bands. Profiles are used in forensic investigations, to compare a sample from a crime scene with samples from suspects, and in paternity testing, where every band in a child's profile must be present in either the mother or the biological father.

A region of DNA that varies in length between individuals, typically a short sequence repeated a different number of times in different people, and that is amplified and measured in a DNA profile. Each marker gives a fragment length that is shared by some proportion of the population, so one marker on its own does not identify a person.

A DNA profile match between two samples that in fact come from different people, arising because the fragment lengths at the markers tested happen to coincide by chance. Increasing the number of independent markers used multiplies together the individual chances of coincidence, so the probability of a false match falls sharply. This is an example of the NOS principle that reliability is enhanced by increasing the number of measurements in a test.

The two ends of a strand of nucleotides, named after the carbon atoms of deoxyribose. At the 5' terminal the fifth carbon of the sugar carries a phosphate group that is not linked to another nucleotide; at the 3' terminal the third carbon carries a free hydroxyl (–OH) group. Because the two strands of a double helix run in opposite directions (antiparallel), the 5' terminal of one strand lies next to the 3' terminal of the other.

DNA polymerases can only add a nucleotide to the 3' terminal of an existing strand: the phosphate on the 5' carbon of the incoming nucleotide is joined to the hydroxyl on the 3' carbon of the last nucleotide in the strand. A new strand therefore grows only in the 5' to 3' direction, and its template is read in the 3' to 5' direction.

The new strand that is synthesized continuously in the same direction as the replication fork moves. Its template runs 3' to 5' towards the fork, so DNA polymerase III can follow the fork adding nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction without interruption. Replication of the leading strand is initiated with an RNA primer only once.

The new strand that is synthesized discontinuously, in short sections, in the direction away from the replication fork. Its template runs 5' to 3' towards the fork, so each section can only be built 5' to 3' away from the fork once enough template has been exposed. Replication of the lagging strand has to be initiated with an RNA primer repeatedly, once for every section.

One of the short lengths of DNA, each begun from its own RNA primer, that make up the lagging strand as it is synthesized. In prokaryotes they are roughly 1000 to 2000 nucleotides long. After the RNA primers have been replaced with DNA, the fragments are joined into one continuous strand.

The enzyme that synthesizes a short RNA primer, complementary to the template, at each point where DNA synthesis is to begin. It is needed because DNA polymerases cannot start a new strand, only extend the 3' terminal of an existing one. In prokaryotes primase acts once at the origin for the leading strand and again at the start of every Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand.

The main replicative enzyme in prokaryotes. Starting from the 3' terminal of an RNA primer, it adds DNA nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction to build the leading strand and each Okazaki fragment of the lagging strand, and it proofreads its own work by removing any mismatched nucleotide it has just added.

The prokaryotic enzyme that removes the RNA nucleotides of each primer and replaces them with DNA nucleotides, extending the 3' terminal of the adjacent DNA. After it has acted, a break (nick) remains in the sugar–phosphate backbone where the last DNA nucleotide it added meets the next fragment.

The enzyme that joins adjacent DNA fragments by forming a covalent bond between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next, sealing the nick left in the backbone after DNA polymerase I has replaced a primer. On the lagging strand it links the Okazaki fragments into a single continuous strand.

The checking of each newly added nucleotide by DNA polymerase III during replication. If the nucleotide just added has a base that is not complementary to the template base, the enzyme removes that nucleotide from the 3' terminal of the growing strand and then adds a correctly matched nucleotide in its place before continuing. Proofreading greatly reduces the error rate of replication but does not eliminate errors altogether.

A base in the newly synthesized strand that is not complementary to the base opposite it on the template, for example a G placed opposite a T. A mismatch that is not removed by proofreading becomes a permanent change in base sequence (a mutation) when the strand is next used as a template.

mcqs.q: A cut in the skin heals as new skin cells are produced by cell division. Why must DNA replication take place before each of these divisions?
options: So that each new cell receives a complete copy of the DNA with an identical base sequence.
So that the existing DNA can be divided equally, half going to each of the new cells.
It does not need to take place, because replication is only required for reproduction.
So that the original DNA can stay intact in one cell and the other cell gets a new copy.
mcqs.specStatementText: Replication makes exact copies, and every dividing cell needs it
mcqs.explain: DNA replication produces exact copies of DNA with identical base sequences. It is required not only for reproduction but for growth and tissue replacement, because every cell produced by division must receive a complete copy.
rationales: DNA replication produces exact copies of DNA with identical base sequences. It is required not only for reproduction but for growth and tissue replacement, because every cell produced by division must receive a complete copy.
A student who thinks division shares out the DNA picks this. The DNA is copied before division so that each new cell receives a complete set, not half of the original.

A student who links replication only with reproduction picks this. Replication is also required for growth and tissue replacement in multicellular organisms, since each new cell needs a full copy of the DNA.
A student who imagines conservative replication picks this. Each daughter molecule contains one original strand and one new strand, so neither cell receives the intact original molecule.

mcqs.q: During replication, a section of a template strand with the base sequence TACGGA is copied. Which statement describes the new strand built on this section?
options: Its sequence is TACGGA, an exact copy of the template strand it was assembled on.
Its sequence is ATGCCT, the complement of the template, held to it by hydrogen bonds.
Its sequence is AUGCCU, because uracil replaces thymine in each newly made strand.
Its sequence is ATGCCT, held to the template by covalent bonds made by DNA polymerase.
mcqs.specStatementText: Each copy keeps one old strand; base pairing keeps the copy accurate
mcqs.explain: Complementary base pairing places A opposite T, T opposite A, G opposite C and C opposite G, so the new strand reads ATGCCT and is held to the template by hydrogen bonds between the paired bases.
rationales: A student who expects the new strand to copy its template directly picks this. The new strand is complementary to the template; it is identical to the strand that was originally paired with the template.
Complementary base pairing places A opposite T, T opposite A, G opposite C and C opposite G, so the new strand reads ATGCCT and is held to the template by hydrogen bonds between the paired bases.
A student who confuses replication with transcription picks this. Replication uses DNA nucleotides, so the new strand contains thymine, not uracil, and has the sequence ATGCCT.

A student who thinks an enzyme bonds the bases together picks this. The bases pair by hydrogen bonds that form spontaneously; DNA polymerase forms covalent bonds along the new strand's backbone, not between bases.

mcqs.q: Bacteria were grown for many generations with only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), so all their DNA was heavy. They were then moved to a medium with only light nitrogen (¹⁴N). After one round of replication, all the DNA had a density midway between heavy and light. After a second round, half the DNA was of this intermediate density and half was light. What do these results show about replication?
options: The original double-stranded molecule stays intact and a completely new molecule is made beside it.
Old and new nucleotides become mixed along both strands of every daughter molecule.
Each daughter molecule keeps one original strand and gains one strand that is newly made.
The DNA is not copied but is shared out equally between the daughter cells at each division.
mcqs.specStatementText: Each copy keeps one old strand; base pairing keeps the copy accurate
mcqs.explain: After one round every molecule is one heavy strand plus one light strand, giving intermediate density. After a second round, the two strands of each intermediate molecule separate again, giving half intermediate and half wholly light molecules. Only semi-conservative replication predicts both results.
rationales: A student who pictures conservative replication picks this. Conservative replication would give heavy and light DNA, never intermediate, after the first round; the observed intermediate density rules it out.

A student who pictures dispersive replication picks this. Mixing would fit the first round, but after the second round all molecules would be of a single, lighter intermediate density; no wholly light DNA would appear.

After one round every molecule is one heavy strand plus one light strand, giving intermediate density. After a second round, the two strands of each intermediate molecule separate again, giving half intermediate and half wholly light molecules. Only semi-conservative replication predicts both results.

A student who thinks DNA is halved at division picks this. If no new DNA were made, no light nitrogen could be incorporated and all the DNA would have stayed heavy; the shift to intermediate and then to light density shows that new strands were synthesized.

mcqs.q: What is the role of helicase in DNA replication?
options: It cuts through the sugar–phosphate backbone so that the two strands can come apart.
It adds free nucleotides to each exposed template strand to assemble the two new strands.
It forms the hydrogen bonds that hold each new nucleotide to its complementary base on the template.
It unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two strands.
mcqs.specStatementText: Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
mcqs.explain: Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the strands so that each can serve as a template for DNA polymerase.
rationales: A student who thinks helicase cuts the DNA picks this. Helicase breaks only the hydrogen bonds between bases; the covalent backbone of each strand stays intact so that it can act as a template.
A student who has swapped the two enzymes picks this. Assembling the new strands is the general role of DNA polymerase, not of helicase.
A student who believes an enzyme must make the base pairs picks this. Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases form spontaneously; helicase breaks hydrogen bonds rather than forming them.
Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the strands so that each can serve as a template for DNA polymerase.

mcqs.q: A drug inhibits helicase but has no effect on DNA polymerase. What will happen to DNA replication in a cell treated with the drug?
options: Replication cannot begin, because the hydrogen bonds between the strands are not broken, so no template strand is exposed.
Replication continues normally, because DNA polymerase unwinds the double helix itself as it copies each strand.
New strands are made but fall off the template, because helicase forms the hydrogen bonds that hold new bases in place.
Cell division continues without replication, because the existing DNA is simply shared between the two daughter cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
mcqs.explain: Helicase is needed to unwind the helix and break the hydrogen bonds between the strands. Without it the strands stay paired, no template is exposed and DNA polymerase has nothing to copy.
rationales: Helicase is needed to unwind the helix and break the hydrogen bonds between the strands. Without it the strands stay paired, no template is exposed and DNA polymerase has nothing to copy.
A student who gives the unwinding job to DNA polymerase picks this. DNA polymerase only assembles new strands on templates that helicase has already exposed.

A student who thinks an enzyme makes the base pairs picks this. Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases form spontaneously; helicase's role is to break them, and without it no strand is even started.
A student who thinks division halves the DNA picks this. Each daughter cell must receive a complete copy of the DNA, so without replication normal division cannot proceed.

mcqs.q: Why is Taq polymerase, rather than a DNA polymerase from human cells, used in the polymerase chain reaction?
options: It is a bacterial enzyme that copies DNA much faster than a human polymerase, so fewer cycles are needed.
It is not denatured at the high temperature used to separate the strands, so it lasts through every cycle.
It separates the two strands of the template by itself, so no helicase has to be added to the reaction mixture.
It can start a new strand anywhere on a bare template, so no primers are needed in the reaction mixture.
mcqs.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
mcqs.explain: Each cycle heats the mixture to about 95°C to separate the strands. Taq polymerase, from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, keeps its shape at this temperature, so it does not have to be replaced after each cycle.
rationales: A student who assumes the special enzyme is chosen for speed picks this. Taq polymerase is used because it is heat-stable; the number of cycles is set by how many copies are wanted, not by enzyme speed.

Each cycle heats the mixture to about 95°C to separate the strands. Taq polymerase, from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, keeps its shape at this temperature, so it does not have to be replaced after each cycle.
A student who expects an enzyme to separate the strands picks this. In PCR the strands are separated by heat, not by any enzyme; the point of Taq polymerase is that it survives this heating.
A student who thinks primers are optional picks this. Like every DNA polymerase, Taq polymerase can only extend an existing strand, so primers are essential in PCR.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the primers in the polymerase chain reaction?
options: They break the hydrogen bonds between the two strands so that the polymerase can reach the template.
They only speed the reaction up, because Taq polymerase could begin a new strand at any point along the bare template.
They bind to sequences either side of the target, giving the polymerase a start point and defining the region copied.
They are identical in sequence to the section being copied, so that the polymerase has an exact copy of it to work from.
mcqs.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
mcqs.explain: The two primers anneal to complementary sequences flanking the target on opposite strands. Taq polymerase can only extend an existing strand, so it extends each primer, and only the DNA between the primers is amplified.
rationales: A student who has not separated the roles of heat and primers picks this. The strands are separated by heating to about 95°C; primers bind to the separated strands only after the mixture has cooled.
A student who thinks primers are optional picks this. No DNA polymerase can begin a strand on its own; without primers Taq polymerase makes no product at all.

The two primers anneal to complementary sequences flanking the target on opposite strands. Taq polymerase can only extend an existing strand, so it extends each primer, and only the DNA between the primers is amplified.

A student who expects copies rather than complements picks this. A primer binds by complementary base pairing to the template, so its sequence is complementary to the template, and the polymerase copies the template, not the primer.

mcqs.q: A PCR reaction starts with 10 double-stranded DNA molecules of the target section. How many double-stranded molecules of the target are present after 3 complete cycles?
mcqs.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
mcqs.explain: Every molecule is copied in every cycle, so the number doubles each cycle: 10 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 10 × 2³ = 80.
rationales: A student who thinks each cycle produces a fixed two copies per starting molecule picks this (10 × 2 × 3). Each cycle doubles the whole population, so the growth is 2ⁿ, not 2n.

A student who adds one new copy per starting molecule per cycle and forgets the originals, or who simply multiplies by the number of cycles, picks this. Doubling three times gives 8 times the start, not 3 times.
A student who adds one copy per starting molecule in each cycle picks this (10 + 3 × 10). Copies are themselves copied in later cycles, so the number doubles each time.
Every molecule is copied in every cycle, so the number doubles each cycle: 10 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 10 × 2³ = 80.

mcqs.q: Three DNA fragments of 200, 500 and 1200 base pairs are loaded into the same well of a gel and a voltage is applied. Which statement describes the result?
options: The 200 base pair fragment moves furthest through the gel, towards the positive electrode.
The 1200 base pair fragment moves furthest, because it carries the most negative charge and is pulled harder.
The 200 base pair fragment moves furthest, towards the negative electrode at the far end of the gel.
The three fragments separate according to their base sequences rather than by their lengths.
mcqs.specStatementText: PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
mcqs.explain: All DNA fragments are negatively charged and move towards the positive electrode. The gel acts as a sieve, so the shortest fragment passes through its pores most easily and travels furthest in the time available.
rationales: All DNA fragments are negatively charged and move towards the positive electrode. The gel acts as a sieve, so the shortest fragment passes through its pores most easily and travels furthest in the time available.
A student who reasons from total charge picks this. Charge per unit length is the same for every fragment; the gel holds back longer fragments, so the largest moves least.
A student who has the electrodes reversed picks this. DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so all fragments move towards the positive electrode.
A student who thinks the gel reads the sequence picks this. Fragments of equal length travel equally far whatever their sequence; the gel separates by size only.

mcqs.q: A DNA profile was prepared for a mother, her child and a man who may be the father. The fragment lengths (in base pairs) in each profile were: mother 100, 220, 260, 340; child 100, 150, 220, 300; man 150, 180, 300, 330. What can be concluded?
options: The man is excluded as the father, because two of his bands (180 and 330) do not appear in the child's profile.
The man cannot be excluded as the father: the child's two bands not from the mother (150 and 300) are both in his profile.
The man is excluded as the father, because the child's profile does not match his profile completely.
The man is proved to be the father, because DNA profiles are unique and two of his bands match the child's.
mcqs.specStatementText: Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
mcqs.explain: The child's bands 100 and 220 came from the mother. The remaining bands, 150 and 300, must come from the biological father, and both appear in the man's profile, so he cannot be excluded. Further markers would be used to make the conclusion more reliable.
rationales: A student who expects the child to carry all of the father's bands picks this. A child inherits only half of each parent's DNA, so bands in the father that the child did not inherit are expected.

The child's bands 100 and 220 came from the mother. The remaining bands, 150 and 300, must come from the biological father, and both appear in the man's profile, so he cannot be excluded. Further markers would be used to make the conclusion more reliable.
A student who applies forensic-style complete matching to paternity picks this. Only the child's bands that are not explained by the mother need to be present in the father.
A student who treats any match as proof picks this. Sharing bands at a few markers is consistent with paternity but does not prove it; other men could share the same fragment lengths by chance.

mcqs.q: A forensic laboratory compares a sample from a crime scene with a suspect's DNA using 20 different markers rather than one. Why does this make the result more reliable?
options: One marker is already conclusive, because everyone's DNA is unique; extra markers only make the bands easier to read.
Testing 20 markers is equivalent to repeating a single marker 20 times, and repeating a measurement makes it more accurate.
Each extra independent marker multiplies down the chance that an unrelated person matches by coincidence.
With 20 markers the whole base sequence of the suspect's genome is read, so the identification is made complete.
mcqs.specStatementText: Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
mcqs.explain: The chance that an unrelated person matches at one marker might be a few per cent; the chances at independent markers multiply together, so with 20 markers a false match becomes extremely improbable. This is the NOS principle that reliability is enhanced by increasing the number of measurements.
rationales: A student who transfers the uniqueness of a whole genome to a single marker picks this. Each marker is shared by a proportion of the population, so one marker gives many chance matches.

A student who reads 'more measurements' as 'repeat the same measurement' picks this. Repeating one marker gives the same lengths each time and does not change the chance that another person shares them.

The chance that an unrelated person matches at one marker might be a few per cent; the chances at independent markers multiply together, so with 20 markers a false match becomes extremely improbable. This is the NOS principle that reliability is enhanced by increasing the number of measurements.
A student who thinks profiling reads DNA sequences picks this. A profile compares fragment lengths at a small number of variable regions; it does not read the base sequence of the genome.

mcqs.q: During replication, how does DNA polymerase add each new nucleotide to the strand it is building?
options: It joins the 3' hydroxyl of the incoming nucleotide to the 5' terminal of the growing strand, so that the strand grows in the 3' to 5' direction.
It adds to whichever terminal faces the fork, so both new strands grow in the same direction as the replication fork moves.
It forms hydrogen bonds between the incoming nucleotide and the template base, which then hold the nucleotide in the strand.
It joins the 5' phosphate of the incoming nucleotide to the 3' terminal of the growing strand, so the strand grows in the 5' to 3' direction.
mcqs.specStatementText: Strands have 5' and 3' ends, and polymerase builds one way only
mcqs.explain: The phosphate on the 5' carbon of the incoming nucleotide bonds to the free hydroxyl on the 3' carbon of the last nucleotide in the strand. Growth is therefore only at the 3' terminal, in the 5' to 3' direction, while the template is read 3' to 5'.
rationales: A student who takes the direction the template is read as the direction of synthesis picks this. DNA polymerase can only add to the 3' terminal, so the new strand grows 5' to 3'.
A student who pictures the two strands as parallel picks this. The strands are antiparallel and DNA polymerase adds only to a 3' terminal, so only one new strand can grow towards the fork.

A student who thinks the enzyme makes the base pair picks this. The hydrogen bonds to the template form spontaneously; DNA polymerase forms the covalent bond that links the nucleotide's 5' phosphate to the 3' terminal of the strand.

The phosphate on the 5' carbon of the incoming nucleotide bonds to the free hydroxyl on the 3' carbon of the last nucleotide in the strand. Growth is therefore only at the 3' terminal, in the 5' to 3' direction, while the template is read 3' to 5'.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly compares replication on the leading strand with replication on the lagging strand?
options: The leading strand is made continuously towards the fork; the lagging strand discontinuously, as Okazaki fragments.
The leading strand is made in the 5' to 3' direction, while the lagging strand is made in the opposite, 3' to 5', direction.
Both new strands are made continuously towards the fork, because the two template strands run in the same direction.
The lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments because helicase cuts its template strand into short pieces.
mcqs.specStatementText: Leading strand is built continuously, lagging strand in fragments
mcqs.explain: The leading strand's template runs 3' to 5' towards the fork, so its new strand is built continuously behind the fork. The lagging strand is built in short Okazaki fragments, each 5' to 3' away from the fork, and each needing its own RNA primer.
rationales: The leading strand's template runs 3' to 5' towards the fork, so its new strand is built continuously behind the fork. The lagging strand is built in short Okazaki fragments, each 5' to 3' away from the fork, and each needing its own RNA primer.

A student who thinks the difference between the strands is the direction of synthesis picks this. Both strands are made 5' to 3'; the lagging strand is different because that direction points away from the fork.
A student who pictures parallel strands picks this. The templates are antiparallel, and since DNA polymerase adds only to a 3' terminal, one strand must be made discontinuously, away from the fork.

A student who thinks helicase cuts DNA picks this. Helicase breaks only hydrogen bonds and both templates stay intact; the fragments arise because the lagging strand can only be built in short lengths away from the fork.

mcqs.q: Starting from the origin, one replication fork in a bacterium copies a 6000 base pair section of the chromosome. Okazaki fragments in this bacterium are about 1000 nucleotides long. Approximately how many RNA primers are needed at this fork?
options: One: replication has to be initiated with an RNA primer only once, at the origin, for the whole fork.
About seven: one on the leading strand plus one for each of the six or so Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
Two: one to start each of the two new strands, which are both built continuously to the end of the section.
About twelve: one for each of about six Okazaki fragments on each of the two new strands being made at the fork.
mcqs.specStatementText: Leading strand is built continuously, lagging strand in fragments
mcqs.explain: The leading strand is initiated with an RNA primer only once. The lagging strand is initiated repeatedly, once per Okazaki fragment: 6000 ÷ 1000 gives about six fragments, so about six primers. The total is about seven.
rationales: A student who thinks a primer only starts replication picks this. DNA polymerase III cannot start a strand, so every Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand needs its own primer.

The leading strand is initiated with an RNA primer only once. The lagging strand is initiated repeatedly, once per Okazaki fragment: 6000 ÷ 1000 gives about six fragments, so about six primers. The total is about seven.
A student who treats both strands alike picks this. Only the leading strand is continuous; the lagging strand is made in about six fragments, each beginning with a primer.
A student who thinks both strands are made in fragments picks this. The leading strand is continuous and needs a single primer; only the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments.

mcqs.q: What is the function of DNA polymerase I in prokaryotic DNA replication?
options: It synthesizes most of the new DNA on both strands, being the first polymerase to act at the fork.
It joins the sugar–phosphate backbones of adjacent Okazaki fragments to make one continuous lagging strand.
It removes the RNA nucleotides of each primer and replaces them with DNA nucleotides, filling the gap.
It synthesizes the short DNA primer that DNA polymerase III needs at the start of each fragment.
mcqs.specStatementText: Four prokaryotic enzymes: primase, polymerase III, polymerase I, ligase
mcqs.explain: DNA polymerase I removes each RNA primer and fills the gap with DNA nucleotides, extending the 3' terminal of the adjacent DNA. DNA ligase then seals the remaining nick.
rationales: A student who reads 'I' as the main enzyme picks this. The bulk of DNA synthesis on both strands is carried out by DNA polymerase III.
A student who blurs the polymerases with ligase picks this. Sealing the nick between fragments is the function of DNA ligase, which acts after DNA polymerase I has replaced the primer.
DNA polymerase I removes each RNA primer and fills the gap with DNA nucleotides, extending the 3' terminal of the adjacent DNA. DNA ligase then seals the remaining nick.
A student who thinks the primer is DNA made by a DNA polymerase picks this. The primer is RNA, made by DNA primase; DNA polymerase I removes it rather than making it.

mcqs.q: On the lagging strand, DNA polymerase III has extended an Okazaki fragment until it reaches the RNA primer of the previous fragment. Which sequence of events completes this section of the strand?
options: DNA ligase joins the new fragment to the RNA primer, and then DNA polymerase I replaces the primer with DNA nucleotides.
DNA polymerase III removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA nucleotides, and then DNA ligase joins the two fragments.
DNA primase replaces its RNA primer with DNA nucleotides, and then DNA ligase joins the two fragments together.
DNA polymerase I replaces the RNA primer with DNA nucleotides, and then DNA ligase joins the two fragments together.
mcqs.specStatementText: Four prokaryotic enzymes: primase, polymerase III, polymerase I, ligase
mcqs.explain: DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA, leaving a nick in the backbone between the last nucleotide it added and the next fragment. DNA ligase then forms the covalent bond that seals the nick.
rationales: A student who thinks the fragments must be joined as soon as they meet picks this. DNA ligase acts last: it seals the nick only after the primer has been replaced with DNA.
A student who credits DNA polymerase III with every polymerase task picks this. Removing and replacing primers is the function of DNA polymerase I, not of DNA polymerase III.
A student who takes DNA primase to be a DNA-making enzyme picks this. Primase makes RNA primers only; it is DNA polymerase I that removes them and replaces them with DNA.

DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA, leaving a nick in the backbone between the last nucleotide it added and the next fragment. DNA ligase then forms the covalent bond that seals the nick.

mcqs.q: As DNA polymerase III builds a new strand it adds a nucleotide carrying G opposite a T on the template. What happens next?
options: DNA polymerase III removes the G nucleotide from the 3' terminal and adds an A in its place.
Synthesis continues, and the mismatch is found and corrected once the whole molecule has been copied.
DNA polymerase III removes the mismatched nucleotide from the 5' terminal of the new strand and replaces it.
DNA polymerase I, the enzyme that removes nucleotides, cuts out the mismatched G and replaces it with an A.
mcqs.specStatementText: Polymerase III checks each nucleotide as it adds it
mcqs.explain: Proofreading is the action of DNA polymerase III in removing any nucleotide with a mismatched base from the 3' terminal of the growing strand and replacing it with a correctly matched nucleotide, here A opposite T, before continuing.
rationales: Proofreading is the action of DNA polymerase III in removing any nucleotide with a mismatched base from the 3' terminal of the growing strand and replacing it with a correctly matched nucleotide, here A opposite T, before continuing.

A student who pictures proofreading as a scan of the finished molecule picks this. DNA polymerase III can only remove the nucleotide at the 3' terminal, so the mismatch is dealt with before synthesis continues.
A student who muddles the two terminals picks this. The nucleotide just added is at the 3' terminal, the growing end of the strand, and that is where DNA polymerase III removes it.
A student who generalizes DNA polymerase I as the removal enzyme picks this. DNA polymerase I removes RNA primers; proofreading of a just-added nucleotide is done by DNA polymerase III itself.

mcqs.q: A mutant strain of Escherichia coli has a DNA polymerase III that can add nucleotides normally but cannot remove them. Which prediction about this strain is correct?
options: Nothing changes, because complementary base pairing on its own ensures that every nucleotide added is correct.
Its mutation rate rises, because mismatched nucleotides at the 3' terminal are left in place and copied in later replications.
Nothing changes, because DNA polymerase I proofreads the new strand once DNA polymerase III has finished with it.
Nothing changes, because mismatches are found and corrected by a separate check of the whole molecule after replication is complete.
mcqs.specStatementText: Polymerase III checks each nucleotide as it adds it
mcqs.explain: Proofreading depends on DNA polymerase III removing a mismatched nucleotide from the 3' terminal. Without this, occasional mismatches from base pairing errors remain in the new strand and are copied as permanent changes in sequence.
rationales: A student who believes base pairing is infallible picks this. A wrong nucleotide is occasionally added; proofreading is what removes most of these, so losing it raises the error rate.

Proofreading depends on DNA polymerase III removing a mismatched nucleotide from the 3' terminal. Without this, occasional mismatches from base pairing errors remain in the new strand and are copied as permanent changes in sequence.

A student who assigns the removal job to DNA polymerase I picks this. DNA polymerase I does not check the strand that polymerase III has built; its function in replication is to replace the RNA primers. Each added nucleotide is proofread by DNA polymerase III itself, and strains lacking this activity have greatly raised mutation rates.

A student who pictures proofreading as a post-replication scan picks this. In the scope of D1.1.9 the only correction is DNA polymerase III removing a just-added mismatched nucleotide from the 3' terminal; without that activity the mismatch remains.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D1.1 DNA replication

specStatements.text: Replication makes exact copies, and every dividing cell needs it
Each copy keeps one old strand; base pairing keeps the copy accurate
Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
PCR copies a chosen DNA section; electrophoresis sorts fragments by length
Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
Strands have 5' and 3' ends, and polymerase builds one way only
Leading strand is built continuously, lagging strand in fragments
Four prokaryotic enzymes: primase, polymerase III, polymerase I, ligase
Polymerase III checks each nucleotide as it adds it

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every object anchored to D1.1.3 treats helicase only as the enzyme that unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between strands, and DNA polymerase only as the enzyme that assembles a new complementary strand on a template. DNA gyrase, single-stranded binding proteins, primase, ligase, the numbered polymerases and 5'/3' directionality are kept out of all SL objects and appear only in HL objects anchored to D1.1.6 to D1.1.9.

The four enzymes are described and tested only as they act in bacterial (Escherichia coli) replication: DNA primase, DNA polymerase I, DNA polymerase III and DNA ligase. Eukaryotic polymerases (alpha, delta, epsilon), telomerase, multiple origins and the eukaryotic enzymes that remove primers are not mentioned.

Proofreading is presented solely as DNA polymerase III removing a just-added mismatched nucleotide from the 3' terminal of the growing strand and replacing it. Post-replication mismatch repair (MutS/MutL), excision repair, the proofreading activity of DNA polymerase I and the term 'exonuclease' as a named activity are not included.
